dossier.summary: The paper is a simulation study of how accurate the regression-based GATE estimator is under network interference. It finds a variance law in the harmonic-mean degree, an n-independent bias floor under a nonlinear exposure response, design and estimator trade-offs across synthetic and two real Facebook graphs, predictable biases under three model mismatches, and badly under-covering HC1 intervals. The numbers in the text and tables trace to delivered result tables written by analysis runs in the record, and the closed-form predictions (bias floor, count-channel and two-hop biases) agree closely with simulation. Support is weaker in a few places: the 'iid' variance-law configurations still carry a degree loading, the 'cluster designs hurt on real graphs' finding rests on one graph and a baseline tied to the randomised clusters, the stated reason for lin_count's error is misattributed, and the claim that the oracle is a lower bound is contradicted by 43 of 80 E2 settings. Uncertainty is reported as replicate bootstrap intervals that, as the paper says, ignore population-level variation. The study does not try multi-stage or multi-ratio designs, GNN regressors or dynamic graphs.

claims.quote: For a linear-in-exposure model under Bernoulli randomisation, sampling SD follows $\hat\sigma\sqrt{(1+\dH)/(np(1-p))}$, with $\dH$ the harmonic-mean degree; this matched simulation within about 10\% when baseline outcomes are unrelated to network position
scope_words: when baseline outcomes are unrelated to network position

claims.quote: but underpredicted the SD by a factor of about 1.6--7 when baselines are community-correlated on clustered graphs or degree-correlated on hub-heavy real graphs
With a nonlinear exposure response, the linear estimator has an $n$-independent bias floor that an exact binomial formula predicts (corr.\ 0.995, 80 synthetic settings)
flexible fits remove it but multiply variance
Cluster randomisation helps substantially on strongly clustered synthetic graphs but can hurt on real ones (Stanford3).
Mis-specified interference structure produces predictable biases (neighbour-count channel, two-hop spillover, missing edges)
heteroskedasticity-robust CIs under-cover badly (down to 0.18) where a two-hop network-robust variant recovers 0.86--0.95 under Bernoulli designs
showing that no estimator or design is uniformly best and that the benefit of cluster designs differs sharply across graphs (large on SBM/WS, negative on Stanford3)
scope_words: no estimator or design is uniformly best

claims.quote: In our simulations error is governed by three quantities: the extrapolation leverage $\Delta^2$ (set by $p$, harmonic degree and, via clusters, the exposure range), the exposure-response curvature relative to what the design reveals (bias floor), and the match between the analyst's exposure model and the true mechanism.

Adding degree and count features (\texttt{lin\_both}) removed the inflation: its SD was 0.06--0.11 on all E7 settings, close to the no-loading value, so the variance blow-up is explainable by omitted position covariates, not by the extrapolation per se.
scope_words: not by the extrapolation per se

issues.quote: (6) The analyst's graph is exact except in E5, and the oracle estimator uses the true $s$ so is a lower bound on achievable error.
issues.why: In code/tables/E2_metrics.csv the misspecified lin_frac has lower RMSE than oracle_h in 43 of the 80 synthetic grid settings (e.g. ER d=40, s=16, p=0.1: rRMSE 0.51 vs 5.94; BA d=10, s=8, p=0.25: 0.074 vs 0.146), so oracle_h is not a lower bound; the paper concedes one such case in Section 5.2, which is why this is minor.

issues.quote: whereas the count-only model (\texttt{lin\_count}) is wrong under the fraction model and has rRMSE up to 1.3 on ER; analysts therefore cannot pick the exposure feature from first principles.
issues.why: lin_count was only run in the count-channel configurations (run_experiments.py lines 90-94), where its exposure feature is the true one; the rRMSE of 1.32 (E5_count.csv, er30) comes from the degree-loaded baseline confounding the count feature, not from a fraction-model mismatch, so the stated reason and the lesson drawn from it are not what the files show.

issues.quote: Louvain clusters on Stanford3 retain 28\% of edges within clusters vs.\ 89\% in our SBM, and the cluster-level baseline effects ($\mathrm{sd}=1$) make the effective sample size about the number of clusters (151).
issues.why: The explanation for why cluster randomisation hurts on Stanford3 is not isolated by any run: community-effect SD and cluster granularity are never varied in E3, and the community effect is drawn on the very clusters that are randomised. The paper notes that granularity was not tuned (Limitation 4).

issues.quote: Cluster randomisation helps substantially on strongly clustered synthetic graphs but can hurt on real ones (Stanford3).
issues.why: 'Real ones' rests on one of the two real graphs (on ego-Facebook cluster randomisation helps, 0.20 vs 0.39), on one Louvain partition per graph, and on a baseline whose community effect sits on the randomised clusters, so this is a property of the simulated outcome model as much as of real graphs.

issues.quote: where the exposure $f_i$ is spatially smooth and nearly collinear with the community effect
issues.why: The collinearity explanation for the 1.6-3.9x SD inflation on WS/SBM is asserted, not measured (no correlation between exposure and community effect is reported or varied).

issues.quote: On BA graphs, whose degrees are heavy-tailed, the harmonic mean matters: mean ratio 0.95 with $\dH$ vs.\ 0.82 with the mean degree; on ER/WS/SBM the two differ by at most 5 percentage points
issues.why: On ER and SBM the gap is 5.4 and 5.5 points, and there the mean-degree version is closer to 1 (0.99 vs 1.05 on ER; 1.02 vs 1.08 on SBM; results/extra_stats.log); the case for the harmonic mean over the mean degree rests on BA alone.

issues.quote: this matched simulation within about 10\% when baseline outcomes are unrelated to network position
issues.why: The largest deviation over the iid-baseline configurations is 13% (WS/SBM max 1.13, ER/BA min 0.91; Table 1), and these 'iid' configurations still carry the default log-degree loading of 0.5 (core.py line 40), so the baselines are not unrelated to network position.

issues.quote: flexible fits remove it but multiply variance
issues.why: GBM keeps relative biases of -0.07 to -0.13 on synthetic Bernoulli designs at s=4 and the spline has -0.07 to -0.11 on ER/SBM at s=8 (E3_analysis.log), so the flexible fits reduce the bias floor rather than remove it.

issues.quote: The ``best feasible'' estimator changes with graph, design and $s$ (\texttt{tables/E3\_best.csv}).
issues.why: Several cells of E3_best.csv are decided by differences far below the replicate-level bootstrap error (e.g. WS cluster s=4: gbm 0.089 vs lin_frac 0.089; SBM10 cluster s=4: spline 0.102 vs lin_frac 0.102). Large reversals (spline on Stanford3 vs ER) still support the general point.

issues.quote: Estimators with data-driven selection (e.g.\ \citealp{han2023}) were not compared; \texttt{spline}/\texttt{gbm} use fixed hyperparameters.
issues.why: The flexible regressions are untuned (fixed knots, fixed GBM settings) and no model-selection or GNN regression is compared, which limits the comparison behind 'no estimator is uniformly best'. The paper states this.

issues.quote: Monte-Carlo uncertainty comes from a bootstrap over replicates (a caveat: only 3--4 graph/noise populations per configuration, so population-to-population variability is not captured by these intervals).
issues.why: Intervals reflect only assignment randomness. On the real graphs all populations share one graph and one Louvain partition, and coverage values in Table 2 carry no Monte-Carlo error. The paper states the caveat.

presentation.why: Figure 3's heatmap prints its cell values and row labels at about 3-4 pt; at print size most rRMSE values cannot be read without zooming.
Figure 5's legend (fontsize 5) and the overlapping line styles make the nine design/estimator series hard to tell apart.
No figure shows the setup (outcome model, designs, estimators, experiment families E1-E7); the reader assembles it from Sections 3-4 and Appendix B.

The text cites internal file paths and column names (tables/E1_varlaw.csv, tables/E3_metrics.csv, tables/E6_coverage.csv, covps_* columns) and run-history details (the E1-E7 ids with no E4; the overwritten n=64,000 run in Limitation 7).
The heading of Appendix D ('Sample-size and noise sweeps') has no text, and its only figure floats above the heading under Appendix C.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: show that when baseline outcomes are iid, the empirical SD equals the \cref{prop:var} prediction within about 10\%
paper_mismatches.why: E1 configs set only comm_sd, so deg_coef keeps its default 0.5 (gate/core.py line 40): the 'iid baseline' rows of Table 1 have baselines loaded on standardised log-degree.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: cluster randomisation (Louvain clusters \citep{blondel2008}, whole clusters assigned with $p{=}0.5$)
paper_mismatches.why: For SBM graphs the planted blocks, not Louvain communities, are used as randomisation clusters and community-effect units, so the SBM cluster designs use the true partition. That is a best case for the 'cluster randomisation helps' result.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Each configuration uses 3--4 independently generated populations (graph and baseline noise)
paper_mismatches.why: For Stanford3 and ego-Facebook every population uses the same graph and the same Louvain partition (seed 0); only the baseline draw changes between populations.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: SE-ratio = within-population empirical SD / mean HC1 SE.
paper_mismatches.why: Table 2 divides the pooled SD (r.sd), not sd_pop; the edit that was meant to switch to sd_pop did not take effect. The two differ by at most 0.001 here.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Empirical SD of $\hat\tau$ divided by the \cref{prop:var} prediction (mean [min, max] over configurations; E1, E7).
paper_mismatches.why: E7 rows plug in the population baseline variance mean(res^2), while E1 rows plug in the regression residual variance s2. Table 1 therefore mixes two versions of the prediction (e.g. ego-Facebook loading 1.0: 7.08 here vs 7.13 with the E1 plug-in in the record).

problems.why: The raw replicate files results/*_reps.csv.gz that every analysis script loads were not delivered (MANIFEST left_out), so tables and figures cannot be regenerated without re-running the ~2-3 h simulation.
Dependencies and versions are listed only in README prose; there is no requirements or environment file.
data/get_data.sh downloads ego-Facebook; facebook_combined.txt.gz is not in the delivery, so the E1-E3, E5-E7 configurations on ego-Facebook need network access.
run_all.sh says ~3-4 h for the simulations while README says 2-3 h total.

process_notes: The simulations for E1, E2 (first run), E3, E5 and E6 ran inside job:all_experiments and job:E6E5E3, which tables.json does not mark as program runs; only job:E7 and job:E2rerun count as experiment runs above.
E2 ran twice: the first run (103 configs, including n=64,000) finished, but the re-run without n=64,000 overwrote its outputs. The paper states this (Limitation 7).
E7 was added after E1 showed the variance law failing on real graphs (step 33) and is reported as a diagnostic.
The sandbox rewrote ' / ' as ' . ' inside shell heredocs. One planned fix, Table 2 using sd_pop, silently did not apply.
Rework: analyze_E3.py was re-run after the paper draft (step 143) to save tables/E3_best.csv, which the text cites.
Smoke-test and --quick outputs were deleted, as the README says.

integrity.why: No tuning or choice of a reported configuration by score: estimators and designs were fixed in run_experiments.py before the runs. The 'best feasible' table only describes results and excludes the oracle. Score comparisons in the record were used to check the paper's text.

The changes during the work were adding the E7 diagnostic after the E1 results (reported as E7), re-running E2 without n=64,000 after a stalled run (stated in Limitation 7), an attempted SE-ratio change that did not apply, and figure rescaling. Text edits moved the paper's numbers toward the files and softened claims. None changes a metric or split to favour a result.
The estimators see only (z, y, analyst graph). The true tau enters only the error metrics. The true nonlinearity s is used only by oracle_h, which the paper labels as an infeasible reference.

All checked paper numbers trace to tables/logs written by analysis runs on simulation outputs. The LaTeX tables come from make_paper_tables.py. The prose numbers were typed by hand but match these files up to rounding, apart from the items listed under issues. The lost n=64,000 point is not reported.
